patient.chief_complaint: Progressive behavioral changes and judicial performance decline — 28 months; referred by occupational health after judicial performance review
patient.history_present_illness: The Honorable Judge W is a 63-year-old retired judge who presents with her husband of 36 years. The referral comes from the occupational health physician of the judicial system, who describes a 28-month history of progressive behavioral and professional decline that led to a confidential judicial performance review and ultimately to her retirement 18 months ago. Her husband is the primary historian as she dismisses all concerns with judicial formality, stating she 'retired on her own terms' and 'has no medical problems worth discussing.' Her husband reports that the behavioral changes began approximately 28 months ago, initially attributed to the stress of a high-profile murder case. She began making errors in legal proceedings that were out of character — contradicting written rulings made minutes earlier, making statements to litigants that her colleagues found highly inappropriate, and once dismissing a case for a reason that had no legal basis. Outside the courtroom, she began purchasing identical items online without recollection — 14 dresses, 22 identical coffee mugs, and several expensive collectibles she had no prior interest in. She made sexually suggestive comments to a church elder in front of congregation members, causing a significant incident. She has developed a fixed daily routine and becomes highly distressed when any element is altered. She repeats the same three stories at dinner parties, word for word, without awareness of repetition. She has lost interest in her family's activities and shows no emotional engagement with her grandchildren whom she previously adored. Her mother has Alzheimer's disease (diagnosed at age 72 — currently in memory care). Her brother has uncharacterized memory complaints. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c on recent check) and hypertension — both vascular risk factors that could contribute to white matter disease. She has well-controlled hypothyroidism. The DIAGNOSTIC TRAP in this case: (1) family history of maternal AD raises familial Alzheimer's concern; (2) vascular risk factors raise vascular dementia; (3) the behavioral syndrome (disinhibition, perseveration, loss of empathy) is FTD pattern, not AD pattern. The key investigation that resolves the case: negative amyloid PET excludes maternal AD inheritance; FDG-PET frontal pattern excludes vascular dementia.

results.title: FDG-PET distinguishes bvFTD from vascular dementia: frontal vs subcortical-frontal metabolic patterns

output.summary: Vascular dementia (subcortical small vessel type) produces a characteristic FDG-PET pattern of subcortical and periventricular hypometabolism corresponding to white matter hyperintensities, with relative preservation of cortical metabolism. The degree of metabolic change is generally proportional to the volume of white matter lesions. In this patient: Fazekas 2 white matter would produce modest subcortical hypometabolism — the 28-32% frontal cortical hypometabolism is far in excess of what Fazekas 2 alone would produce. The severe frontal cortical metabolic reduction is a primary neurodegenerative (FTD) pattern, not a secondary vascular white matter effect. The preserved posterior cortex further distinguishes bvFTD from both AD and strategic vascular dementia.

results.title: Frontotemporal dementia in professional occupations: occupational performance and ethical implications

output.summary: bvFTD in professionals with decision-making authority (judges, physicians, attorneys, executives) creates unique ethical and legal issues. Key considerations: (1) judicial decisions made during the period of undetected bvFTD may be subject to review — medical documentation can support appeals in affected cases; (2) formal capacity assessment for all ongoing decisions is mandatory; (3) power of attorney (financial and healthcare) must be established urgently; (4) driving cessation must be addressed — bvFTD impairs risk judgment critical for driving safety; (5) financial capacity is impaired (the repeated online purchases indicate this); (6) confidential disclosure to judicial oversight bodies may be required depending on jurisdiction — ethical and legal consultation is warranted.

key_reasoning_points: APOE e4 is the most common genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease but is NOT diagnostic — it increases lifetime risk but many APOE e4 carriers never develop AD; negative amyloid PET is the definitive exclusion test
